newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Security Council set to okay troops in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Security Council set to okay troops in Zaire.

text.p: The United Nations Security Council on Friday met to authorise a force to ensure humanitarian aid reaches more than a million refugees in eastern Zaire as hundreds of thousands of them began trekking home to Rwanda.

In a resolution, sponsored by 30 countries and expected to be adopted unanimously, the 15-member body was to approve the Canadian-led force for Zaire until March 31 to allow relief workers to feed the refugees, many of whom have also fled west into the Zairean hinterlands.

The resolution gives the troops "all necessary means" to defend themselves. But Canadian Lt Gen. Maurice Baril, the commander of the force, said the troops would not attempt to disarm Hutu militia among the refugees.
Although the force is not under U.N. command, the countries pressing for intervention wanted an international seal of approval for their action.

Troops who are expected to go in first are from the Canada, the United States, Britain, France, Senegal, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands. Others may follow from Austria, Portugal, Sweden, Ireland, South Africa, Argentina, Brazil, Congo, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Mali, Egypt and Nigeria.
Finland, Norway, Germany and Israel are expected to help with humanitarian aid.

As the council early on Friday was putting the finishing touches on the document, about a third of the more than 1.2 million refugees abandoned camps in Mugunga near Goma and began the exodus to Rwanda.

Consequently Rwanda's U.N. ambassador, Gideon Kayinamura, immediately said the migration meant the force was no longer needed and the world should send aid to his country instead. But chief U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said most of the remaining refugees were without basic necessities and a force was still required.

During the debate, however, Zaire's U.N. envoy, Lubaku Khabouji N'Zaji, said Rwanda did not really want the refugees back. "For two years they have been living like animals and now the Rwandese cabinet goes there to welcome them. The council should not allow itself to be duped by such manoeuvres."
-- authorises the mission under Chapter VII of the U.N. Charter which allows the use of force.
-- ends the operation no later than March 31.
-- calls for a "follow-on" operation, either military or civilian organised by the United Nations, which is to submit its recommendations by January 1.
-- says that costs for the new multinational force would be borne by participating nations but asks Boutros-Ghali to set up a fund for African states to help pay for their troops.

The way was cleared to deploy the force after the United States signalled on Wednesday it was prepared to join the operation with 1,000 troops in Zaire and up to 4,000 additional soldiers as backup in neighbouring countries. The force may have more than 10,000 troops.

Many refugees, mainly Hutus, had been too terrified to return to Rwanda because of intimidation by Hutu militia and out of fear of reprisals by Tutsis, who dominate the government. They fled to Zaire in 1994 after massacres by Hutu militants of the country's Tutsi minority and moderate Hutus..
Hutu fighters, blamed for the genocide of some 800,000 Rwandans, were reported to have fled into the bush, having lost their two-year bid to stop ordinary refugees from leaving.

To induce refugees to return home, the United Nations wants an aid programme within Rwanda feeding areas set up near the Rwandan and Burundi borders, and human rights monitors may be increased in Rwanda from 110 to 300. Relief supplies, including seeds for planting, are to be delivered to Rwanda.
